paper_sections.title: 3.2 Differences in regional activity and connectivity

description.value: The study investigated altered resting-state regional brain activity and seed-based functional connectivity in patients with congenital right-sided unilateral microtia and severe hearing loss, including the effects of global signal regression and associations with clinical variables.

spans.text: To examine the effect of GSR on UM-related functional alterations, rs-fMRI data were analyzed both with and without GSR during preprocessing.

Compared with controls, patients with UM had lower ALFF values in the left temporal pole, superior temporal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and medial prefrontal cortex; and higher ALFF values in the left inferior temporal gyrus and precuneus.

design.value: A retrospective, cross-sectional case-control study comparing resting-state fMRI measures between patients with congenital right-sided unilateral microtia and age- and sex-matched normal-hearing controls, with analyses performed with and without global signal regression.

spans.text: The present study included 27 patients aged 11–40 years with right-sided congenital unilateral microtia (UM group) and 27 age- and sex-matched normal hearing individuals aged 11–35 years (NC group).
To examine the effect of GSR on UM-related functional alterations, rs-fMRI data were analyzed both with and without GSR during preprocessing.
This retrospective study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Peking Union Medical College Hospital (reference number: JS-796).

description.value: Resting-state fMRI images were processed using SPM12 and SeeCAT, including deletion of the first 10 time points, slice-timing and head-motion correction, normalization, resampling, smoothing, nuisance regression, temporal filtering, and scrubbing.

spans.text: All rs-fMRI images were processed using SPM12 ( www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/ ) and SeeCAT ( www.nitrc.org/projects/seecat ) software.
The first 10 time points of the functional imaging were deleted because of the instability of the initial MRI signal and the need for participants to adapt to the scanning environment.
Thereafter, slice-timing and head-motion correction were implemented.
The corrected images were normalized to the EPI template, resampled to 3-mm isotropic voxels, and further smoothed with a 4-mm full-width at half maximum Gaussian kernel.
Confounding signals, including those of white matter and cerebrospinal fluid, as well as linear drift and Friston-24 head-motion parameters, were removed using a linear regression model.
The time series for each voxel was temporally band-pass filtered (0.01–0.1 Hz) to reduce low-frequency drift and physiological high-frequency noise.
Finally, a scrubbing procedure based on framewise indices was utilized to reduce motion-related effects on FC analysis.
